opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the interviews were kind of a turning point for me. I was on the market around the time large models were really taking off, and I'd go from campus to campus giving a job talk on my own research. Almost every meeting, whether it was with a dean or a junior faculty member, eventually came back to the same question: "What do you think about large language models? How does your work relate to them?"

At first I treated it as a distraction. I had a research agenda I was proud of, and I wanted to talk about that. But after the fifth or sixth interview, I realized these weren't polite questions. People were genuinely trying to figure out which parts of the field would still matter in five years. Some senior professors were openly saying, "A lot of what we used to do might get absorbed by scaling." Hearing that from people I respected made a big impression on me.

It also made me look harder at my own work. In those one-on-one meetings you're forced to defend your direction in thirty minutes, and I noticed my answers about where I fit relative to large models weren't very convincing, even to me. That discomfort was useful. It pushed me to actually spend time with the models: reading the papers carefully, running experiments, and trying to understand where they break.

So the interviews didn't change my interest overnight, but they acted like a mirror. They showed me the field was shifting under everyone's feet, and that if I wanted to do work that mattered, I had to engage with large models directly instead of treating them as someone else's topic.

fable-5.1.text:
Kay Ke: It was a pretty formative experience, honestly. When I went on the faculty market, you do this whole tour, maybe fifteen or twenty schools, and at each one you give the same job talk and then sit through a day of one-on-one meetings with faculty. And the thing I kept noticing was that the questions I got in those meetings were changing month by month. Early in the cycle people wanted to talk about my thesis work, the specific problems I'd solved. By the end, almost every conversation drifted toward the same place: what do you make of these large models, and does your research agenda still make sense in a world where scale seems to be eating everything?

At first I found that a little threatening, because I was there to sell a five-year plan, and the honest answer was that I wasn't sure. But the more I had that conversation, the more I realized it was the most interesting question anyone was asking me. I'd walk out of a meeting and keep thinking about it on the way to the next one. Some senior people were very dismissive, this is just engineering, it'll plateau. Others, often the younger faculty, were quietly rethinking everything they worked on. Seeing that split up close, across so many departments, made it clear to me that this wasn't a fad, it was a real shift in what the field considered a good problem.

So in a strange way the interviews converted me. I went in planning to defend a fairly narrow agenda, and I came out convinced that if I didn't engage seriously with large models, I'd be spending my career on the wrong side of the most important thing happening. That's what pushed me to reorient, and it's a big part of why I ended up where I am now rather than in a traditional faculty role.
